hover:text-theme-text-sec block ">Keep review close to the code</a></li></ul></div></div></nav><div class="prose prose--block col-span-full!"><p>Code review is often slow and uneven: diffs wait in queues, and feedback depends on who is online.</p>
<p>AI code review only helps when the reviewer has real codebase context.</p>
<p>AI code review works best when the reviewer already has the full repo, recent changes, tests, and a clear set of rules. AI code review with this context catches problems a standalone bot staring at a single diff will never see. Review is most useful as part of the same system that produced the change.</p>
<h2 id="what-changed-about-code-review" class="anchor-heading group "><a href="#what-changed-about-code-review" class="anchor-link" aria-label="Link to this section"><span class="anchor-icon" aria-hidden="true">#</span></a>What changed about code review</h2>
<p>Coding agents did not invent long pull requests, but they made the old review math fail faster.</p>
<p>Developers working with coding agents are shipping bigger changes. <a href="https://cursor.com/insights/developer-habits" rel="noopener noreferrer" target="_blank">Data from millions of Cursor sessions</a> shows lines added per PR (p75) up about 2.5x year over year. Mega PRs of 1,000+ changed lines are a growing share of merges, with a clear jump in January 2026 as agents and models improved. Agent sessions got deeper too: mean tool calls per session rose about 30% in a recent two-month window. More of the AI-authored code survives. Accepted AI lines still present after 60 minutes rose from roughly 76% to 81% since the start of 2026. Agent-generated changes that reach commits without a separate manual diff-acceptance step grew more than 5x over that period.</p>
<p>Human review capacity did not scale with any of that. Classic peer-review guidance has long treated a few hundred lines of careful reading as the range where quality holds.</p>
<p>AI code review is how you keep a quality gate when the volume of change outruns the number of senior engineers who can read every diff.</p>
<p>More of the code under review was written with AI assistance. Humans are good at catching &quot;this does not match how we build here.&quot; They are worse at staring down a large, plausible, mostly-correct agent patch for the one subtle break, which is where a reviewer with real repo context helps. Writing a large change and checking it are different skills, and review is the check.</p>
<h2 id="questions-before-launching-ai-code-review" class="anchor-heading group "><a href="#questions-before-launching-ai-code-review" class="anchor-link" aria-label="Link to this section"><span class="anchor-icon" aria-hidden="true">#</span></a>Questions before launching AI code review</h2>
<p>If you are evaluating AI code review tools, work through these concepts first.</p>
<h3 id="what-is-ai-code-review" class="anchor-heading group "><a href="#what-is-ai-code-review" class="anchor-link" aria-label="Link to this section"><span class="anchor-icon" aria-hidden="true">#</span></a>What is AI code review?</h3>
<p>AI code review is software that reads a change (usually a pull request, sometimes a local diff) and comments on bugs, regressions, and risk before merge. The useful versions reason over more than the changed lines in front of them. They pull related files, tests, config, and team rules. The weak versions restate the diff in prose or nag about comments and naming.</p>
<figure class="media-border-container overflow-hidden bg-theme-bg"><svg viewBox="0 0 800 420" role="img" aria-labelledby="ai-code-review-context-alt" class="h-auto w-full" style="font-family:var(--font-sans)"><rect width="800" height="420" fill="var(--color-theme-bg)"></rect><text x="40" y="44" font-size="26" letter-spacing="-0.02em" fill="var(--color-theme-fg)">What the reviewer can see</text><rect x="40" y="80" width="340" height="300" rx="4" fill="var(--color-theme-bg)" stroke="var(--color-theme-border-02-5)"></rect><text x="210" y="124" text-anchor="middle" font-size="22" fill="var(--color-theme-fg)">Diff only</text><text x="210" y="156" text-anchor="middle" font-size="16" fill="var(--color-theme-fg)" opacity="0.5">Standalone bot</text><text x="68" y="204" font-size="18" fill="var(--color-theme-fg)">Changed lines</text><text x="68" y="240" font-size="18" fill="var(--color-theme-fg)" opacity="0.45">Style and naming nags</text><text x="68" y="276" font-size="18" fill="var(--color-theme-fg)" opacity="0.45">Restated patch</text><text x="68" y="328" font-size="16" fill="var(--color-theme-fg)" opacity="0.45">Misses breaks elsewhere</text><rect x="420" y="80" width="340" height="300" rx="4" fill="var(--color-theme-fg)"></rect><text x="590" y="124" text-anchor="middle" font-size="22" fill="var(--color-theme-bg)">Full context</text><text x="590" y="156" text-anchor="middle" font-size="16" fill="var(--color-theme-bg)" opacity="0.7">Same system that wrote the change</text><text x="448" y="204" font-size="18" fill="var(--color-theme-bg)">Full repo</text><text x="448" y="240" font-size="18" fill="var(--color-theme-bg)">Tests and recent changes</text><text x="448" y="276" font-size="18" fill="var(--color-theme-bg)">Team and repo rules</text><text x="448" y="328" font-size="16" fill="var(--color-theme-bg)" opacity="0.7">Catches the subtle break</text></svg><figcaption id="ai-code-review-context-alt" class="sr-only">A weak AI reviewer only sees the diff. A useful one also has the repo, tests, recent changes, and team rules.</figcaption></figure>
<h3 id="how-is-it-different-from-linting-or-ci" class="anchor-heading group "><a href="#how-is-it-different-from-linting-or-ci" class="anchor-link" aria-label="Link to this section"><span class="anchor-icon" aria-hidden="true">#</span></a>How is it different from linting or CI?</h3>
<p>Linters and typecheckers encode rules you already know how to write. CI runs the checks you automated. AI review is for the residue: logic errors, race conditions, auth mistakes, breaks a few folders away, and mismatched docs and behavior. It overlaps CI. It does not replace it.</p>
<h3 id="does-ai-code-review-replace-human-review" class="anchor-heading group "><a href="#does-ai-code-review-replace-human-review" class="anchor-link" aria-label="Link to this section"><span class="anchor-icon" aria-hidden="true">#</span></a>Does AI code review replace human review?</h3>
<p>No. It changes what humans spend time on. <a href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TswQeKftnaw" rel="noopener noreferrer" target="_blank">Only about half of human review comments</a> lead to a change in the same PR anyway. Healthy review cultures include fix-forward notes and FYI context. You want to clear high-confidence, machine-tractable bugs so people can stay on architecture, product risk, and tribal knowledge the model does not have yet.</p>
<h3 id="what-makes-ai-review-noisy" class="anchor-heading group "><a href="#what-makes-ai-review-noisy" class="anchor-link" aria-label="Link to this section"><span class="anchor-icon" aria-hidden="true">#</span></a>What makes AI review noisy?</h3>
<p>Noise comes from comments people do not want from a bot. Style nags, vague &quot;add tests&quot; notes with no failing test, and rewrite suggestions that do not catch a bug all train people to ignore the review. Separate what the model can catch from what people actually want it to flag. AI code review should flag real bugs, accidental commits, performance and security issues, and places where the docs and the code disagree. When <a href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TswQeKftnaw" rel="noopener noreferrer" target="_blank">Graphite scoped its AI reviews to that overlap</a>, about 52% of comments led to a code change (roughly the same rate as human reviewers), with downvotes under 4%.</p>
<h3 id="what-should-we-measure" class="anchor-heading group "><a href="#what-should-we-measure" class="anchor-link" aria-label="Link to this section"><span class="anchor-icon" aria-hidden="true">#</span></a>What should we measure?</h3>
<p>Resolution rate: at merge time, was the flagged issue actually fixed in the final code? Resolution rate beats comment volume.</p>
<p>This is also the metric we used to improve Bugbot: <a href="https://cursor.com/blog/building-bugbot" rel="noopener noreferrer" target="_blank">resolution moved from 52% to over 70%</a> across 40 experiments, bugs flagged per run from 0.4 to 0.7, and resolved bugs per PR from roughly 0.2 to about 0.5, across <a href="https://cursor.com/blog/building-bugbot" rel="noopener noreferrer" target="_blank">more than two million PRs reviewed per month</a>. By <a href="https://cursor.com/blog/may-2026-bugbot-changes" rel="noopener noreferrer" target="_blank">May 2026</a>, default-effort resolution had reached about 80% of bugs resolved by merge time. If your resolution falls while comment volume rises, the bot is generating noise.</p>
<p>The <a href="https://cursor.com/dashboard/bugbot" rel="noopener noreferrer" target="_blank">Bugbot dashboard</a> charts resolution rate over time for each repository, alongside the volume of issues found and fixed, so you can see whether reviews are catching real problems and getting resolved before you widen what the bot comments on.</p>
<h3 id="when-should-review-run-locally-on-the-pr-or-both" class="anchor-heading group "><a href="#when-should-review-run-locally-on-the-pr-or-both" class="anchor-link" aria-label="Link to this section"><span class="anchor-icon" aria-hidden="true">#</span></a>When should review run: locally, on the PR, or both?</h3>
<p>Both, with different jobs. Local review (after an agent task, before push) catches issues while context is still warm and the thread does not exist yet. PR review is the team contract: shared rules, shared history, and a shared merge gate. Security-focused passes can sit on either side depending on how you ship.</p>
<h3 id="do-we-need-the-review-tool-to-live-in-the-same-product-as-the-agent" class="anchor-heading group "><a href="#do-we-need-the-review-tool-to-live-in-the-same-product-as-the-agent" class="anchor-link" aria-label="Link to this section"><span class="anchor-icon" aria-hidden="true">#</span></a>Do we need the review tool to live in the same product as the agent?</h3>
<p>You can buy a standalone reviewer. Many teams do. The cost is context switching and a thinner view of how the code was produced. When review runs in the same system that wrote the change, it already knows the open files, the repo map, and the rules you maintain next to the code. Fixes can deep-link back into the editor or spawn an agent with the finding loaded. That loop is hard to fake with a bolt-on.</p>
<h2 id="how-to-run-ai-code-review-in-cursor" class="anchor-heading group "><a href="#how-to-run-ai-code-review-in-cursor" class="anchor-link" aria-label="Link to this section"><span class="anchor-icon" aria-hidden="true">#</span></a>How to run AI code review in Cursor</h2>
<p>Cursor&#x27;s path is local review in the editor, Bugbot on the pull request, then a fix loop that returns you to the same toolchain.</p>
<figure class="media-border-container overflow-hidden bg-theme-bg"><svg viewBox="0 0 800 280" role="img" aria-labelledby="ai-code-review-loop-alt" class="h-auto w-full" locally in the editor, then on the pull request, then back into a fix loop.</figcaption></figure>
<p><strong>Local.</strong> After agent work, run <a href="https://cursor.com/docs/agent/agent-review" rel="noopener noreferrer" target="_blank">Agent Review</a>. You can type <code>/agent-review</code> in the agent input, run it from the Source Control tab to compare local changes against your main branch, or turn on automatic reviews after every commit. Before you push, you can also run Bugbot or a Security Agent locally with the <code>/review-bugbot</code> and <code>/review-security</code> skills. This is where you clear obvious problems while the session still has context.</p>
<p><strong>On the PR.</strong> <a href="https://cursor.com/docs/bugbot" rel="noopener noreferrer" target="_blank">Bugbot</a> reviews pull requests on GitHub, GitLab, and Bitbucket. Encode team invariants in <code>.cursor/BUGBOT.md</code>, plus team rules and repo rules. Learned rules (<code>@cursor remember</code>) fold feedback into future runs. Watch resolution rate in Bugbot Automations before you widen comment categories.</p>
<p><strong>Fix loop.</strong> Findings show up on the PR with paths back into Cursor (Fix in Cursor and Fix in Web). Bugbot Autofix can spawn a Cloud Agent to propose repairs. For security, Cursor&#x27;s <a href="https://cursor.com/docs/security-agents" rel="noopener noreferrer" target="_blank">Security Agents</a> cover the two jobs: Security Reviewer checks PRs before merge, and Vulnerability Scanner scans the codebase at rest.</p>
<p><strong>Start.</strong> The docs cover setup end to end: connecting your repo, choosing which repos and people trigger reviews, effort level, and <code>.cursor/BUGBOT.md</code>. Follow along at <a href="https://cursor.com/docs/bugbot" rel="noopener noreferrer" target="_blank">cursor.com/docs/bugbot</a>.</p>
<h2 id="automate-the-routing-and-sign-off" class="anchor-heading group "><a href="#automate-the-routing-and-sign-off" class="anchor-link" aria-label="Link to this section"><span class="anchor-icon" aria-hidden="true">#</span></a>Automate the routing and sign-off</h2>
<p>Finding bugs is not the whole review job. Two Cursor automations handle the mechanical parts.</p>
<p><strong>Auto-approve low-risk changes.</strong> <a href="https://cursor.com/docs/approval-agents" rel="noopener noreferrer" target="_blank">Approval Agents</a> score each pull request by risk and approve the ones that clear the bar you set. A copy tweak or a config bump can merge without waiting on a human. Anything above your risk threshold is held. Bugbot and Security Agent findings feed that decision, so a risky change does not get waved through.</p>
<p><strong>Route to the right reviewers.</strong> When a PR needs a person, Approval Agents assign reviewers based on the part of the codebase it touches, using per-area routing policies you define. The change goes to the team that owns that code instead of a shared queue.</p>
<h2 id="keep-review-close-to-the-code" class="anchor-heading group "><a href="#keep-review-close-to-the-code" class="anchor-link" aria-label="Link to this section"><span class="anchor-icon" aria-hidden="true">#</span></a>Keep review close to the code</h2>
<p>AI code review is how teams keep a quality gate while agents increase the size and speed of change. The versions that work have repo context, a narrow comment policy, and a metric that tracks whether findings get fixed.</p>
<p>Review belongs close to where the code was produced, with the same rules and the same fix path. Turn <a href="https://cursor.com/docs/bugbot" rel="noopener noreferrer" target="_blank">Bugbot</a> on for a busy repo, watch resolution in <a href="https://cursor.com/automations/from-cursor/bugbot" rel="noopener noreferrer" target="_blank">Bugbot Automations</a> for a week, and only then decide which categories deserve more volume.</p></div><footer class="mt-v2"><p class="type-base"><span class="text-theme-text-sec">Filed under:<!-- --> </span><span class="text-theme-text capitalize">code review</span></p></footer></div></div></div></article><section class="mt-v3 border-theme-border-02 border-t pt-v2"><div class="grid-cursor"><div class="col-span-full xl:col-start-1 xl:col-end-7"><h2 class="type-base text-theme-text mb-v1 xl:sticky xl:top-[var(--site-sticky-top)] xl:mb-0">Related guides</h2></div><div class="col-span-full xl:col-start-7 xl:col-end-19"><div class="grid grid-cols-1 gap-g1"><article class="flex grow-1 flex-col"><a class="card card--text grow-1 flex h-full flex-col no-underline" href="/guides/model-routing"><p class="type-base text-theme-text text-pretty">Model routing: right model, right job, right price</p><p class="type-base text-theme-text-sec mt-v4/12 text-pretty">Model routing sends each request to the model that fits the job, so routine work stops billing at frontier prices. hover:text-theme-text-sec block ">Keep review close to the code</a></li></ul></div></div></nav><div class="prose prose--block col-span-full!"><p>Code review is often slow and uneven: diffs wait in queues, and feedback depends on who is online.</p>
<p>AI code review only helps when the reviewer has real codebase context.</p>
<p>AI code review works best when the reviewer already has the full repo, recent changes, tests, and a clear set of rules. AI code review with this context catches problems a standalone bot staring at a single diff will never see. Review is most useful as part of the same system that produced the change.</p>
<h2 id="what-changed-about-code-review" class="anchor-heading group "><a href="#what-changed-about-code-review" class="anchor-link" aria-label="Link to this section"><span class="anchor-icon" aria-hidden="true">#</span></a>What changed about code review</h2>
<p>Coding agents did not invent long pull requests, but they made the old review math fail faster.</p>
<p>Developers working with coding agents are shipping bigger changes. <a href="https://cursor.com/insights/developer-habits" rel="noopener noreferrer" target="_blank">Data from millions of Cursor sessions</a> shows lines added per PR (p75) up about 2.5x year over year. Mega PRs of 1,000+ changed lines are a growing share of merges, with a clear jump in January 2026 as agents and models improved. Agent sessions got deeper too: mean tool calls per session rose about 30% in a recent two-month window. More of the AI-authored code survives. Accepted AI lines still present after 60 minutes rose from roughly 76% to 81% since the start of 2026. Agent-generated changes that reach commits without a separate manual diff-acceptance step grew more than 5x over that period.</p>
<p>Human review capacity did not scale with any of that. Classic peer-review guidance has long treated a few hundred lines of careful reading as the range where quality holds.</p>
<p>AI code review is how you keep a quality gate when the volume of change outruns the number of senior engineers who can read every diff.</p>
<p>More of the code under review was written with AI assistance. Humans are good at catching &quot;this does not match how we build here.&quot; They are worse at staring down a large, plausible, mostly-correct agent patch for the one subtle break, which is where a reviewer with real repo context helps. Writing a large change and checking it are different skills, and review is the check.</p>
<h2 id="questions-before-launching-ai-code-review" class="anchor-heading group "><a href="#questions-before-launching-ai-code-review" class="anchor-link" aria-label="Link to this section"><span class="anchor-icon" aria-hidden="true">#</span></a>Questions before launching AI code review</h2>
<p>If you are evaluating AI code review tools, work through these concepts first.</p>
<h3 id="what-is-ai-code-review" class="anchor-heading group "><a href="#what-is-ai-code-review" class="anchor-link" aria-label="Link to this section"><span class="anchor-icon" aria-hidden="true">#</span></a>What is AI code review?</h3>
<p>AI code review is software that reads a change (usually a pull request, sometimes a local diff) and comments on bugs, regressions, and risk before merge. The useful versions reason over more than the changed lines in front of them. They pull related files, tests, config, and team rules. The weak versions restate the diff in prose or nag about comments and naming.</p>
<figure class="media-border-container overflow-hidden bg-theme-bg"><svg viewBox="0 0 800 420" role="img" aria-labelledby="ai-code-review-context-alt" class="h-auto w-full" style="font-family:var(--font-sans)"><rect width="800" height="420" fill="var(--color-theme-bg)"></rect><text x="40" y="44" font-size="26" letter-spacing="-0.02em" fill="var(--color-theme-fg)">What the reviewer can see</text><rect x="40" y="80" width="340" height="300" rx="4" fill="var(--color-theme-bg)" stroke="var(--color-theme-border-02-5)"></rect><text x="210" y="124" text-anchor="middle" font-size="22" fill="var(--color-theme-fg)">Diff only</text><text x="210" y="156" text-anchor="middle" font-size="16" fill="var(--color-theme-fg)" opacity="0.5">Standalone bot</text><text x="68" y="204" font-size="18" fill="var(--color-theme-fg)">Changed lines</text><text x="68" y="240" font-size="18" fill="var(--color-theme-fg)" opacity="0.45">Style and naming nags</text><text x="68" y="276" font-size="18" fill="var(--color-theme-fg)" opacity="0.45">Restated patch</text><text x="68" y="328" font-size="16" fill="var(--color-theme-fg)" opacity="0.45">Misses breaks elsewhere</text><rect x="420" y="80" width="340" height="300" rx="4" fill="var(--color-theme-fg)"></rect><text x="590" y="124" text-anchor="middle" font-size="22" fill="var(--color-theme-bg)">Full context</text><text x="590" y="156" text-anchor="middle" font-size="16" fill="var(--color-theme-bg)" opacity="0.7">Same system that wrote the change</text><text x="448" y="204" font-size="18" fill="var(--color-theme-bg)">Full repo</text><text x="448" y="240" font-size="18" fill="var(--color-theme-bg)">Tests and recent changes</text><text x="448" y="276" font-size="18" fill="var(--color-theme-bg)">Team and repo rules</text><text x="448" y="328" font-size="16" fill="var(--color-theme-bg)" opacity="0.7">Catches the subtle break</text></svg><figcaption id="ai-code-review-context-alt" class="sr-only">A weak AI reviewer only sees the diff. A useful one also has the repo, tests, recent changes, and team rules.</figcaption></figure>
<h3 id="how-is-it-different-from-linting-or-ci" class="anchor-heading group "><a href="#how-is-it-different-from-linting-or-ci" class="anchor-link" aria-label="Link to this section"><span class="anchor-icon" aria-hidden="true">#</span></a>How is it different from linting or CI?</h3>
<p>Linters and typecheckers encode rules you already know how to write. CI runs the checks you automated. AI review is for the residue: logic errors, race conditions, auth mistakes, breaks a few folders away, and mismatched docs and behavior. It overlaps CI. It does not replace it.</p>
<h3 id="does-ai-code-review-replace-human-review" class="anchor-heading group "><a href="#does-ai-code-review-replace-human-review" class="anchor-link" aria-label="Link to this section"><span class="anchor-icon" aria-hidden="true">#</span></a>Does AI code review replace human review?</h3>
<p>No. It changes what humans spend time on. <a href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TswQeKftnaw" rel="noopener noreferrer" target="_blank">Only about half of human review comments</a> lead to a change in the same PR anyway. Healthy review cultures include fix-forward notes and FYI context. You want to clear high-confidence, machine-tractable bugs so people can stay on architecture, product risk, and tribal knowledge the model does not have yet.</p>
<h3 id="what-makes-ai-review-noisy" class="anchor-heading group "><a href="#what-makes-ai-review-noisy" class="anchor-link" aria-label="Link to this section"><span class="anchor-icon" aria-hidden="true">#</span></a>What makes AI review noisy?</h3>
<p>Noise comes from comments people do not want from a bot. Style nags, vague &quot;add tests&quot; notes with no failing test, and rewrite suggestions that do not catch a bug all train people to ignore the review. Separate what the model can catch from what people actually want it to flag. AI code review should flag real bugs, accidental commits, performance and security issues, and places where the docs and the code disagree. When <a href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TswQeKftnaw" rel="noopener noreferrer" target="_blank">Graphite scoped its AI reviews to that overlap</a>, about 52% of comments led to a code change (roughly the same rate as human reviewers), with downvotes under 4%.</p>
<h3 id="what-should-we-measure" class="anchor-heading group "><a href="#what-should-we-measure" class="anchor-link" aria-label="Link to this section"><span class="anchor-icon" aria-hidden="true">#</span></a>What should we measure?</h3>
<p>Resolution rate: at merge time, was the flagged issue actually fixed in the final code? Resolution rate beats comment volume.</p>
<p>This is also the metric we used to improve Bugbot: <a href="https://cursor.com/blog/building-bugbot" rel="noopener noreferrer" target="_blank">resolution moved from 52% to over 70%</a> across 40 experiments, bugs flagged per run from 0.4 to 0.7, and resolved bugs per PR from roughly 0.2 to about 0.5, across <a href="https://cursor.com/blog/building-bugbot" rel="noopener noreferrer" target="_blank">more than two million PRs reviewed per month</a>. By <a href="https://cursor.com/blog/may-2026-bugbot-changes" rel="noopener noreferrer" target="_blank">May 2026</a>, default-effort resolution had reached about 80% of bugs resolved by merge time. If your resolution falls while comment volume rises, the bot is generating noise.</p>
<p>The <a href="https://cursor.com/dashboard/bugbot" rel="noopener noreferrer" target="_blank">Bugbot dashboard</a> charts resolution rate over time for each repository, alongside the volume of issues found and fixed, so you can see whether reviews are catching real problems and getting resolved before you widen what the bot comments on.</p>
<h3 id="when-should-review-run-locally-on-the-pr-or-both" class="anchor-heading group "><a href="#when-should-review-run-locally-on-the-pr-or-both" class="anchor-link" aria-label="Link to this section"><span class="anchor-icon" aria-hidden="true">#</span></a>When should review run: locally, on the PR, or both?</h3>
<p>Both, with different jobs. Local review (after an agent task, before push) catches issues while context is still warm and the thread does not exist yet. PR review is the team contract: shared rules, shared history, and a shared merge gate. Security-focused passes can sit on either side depending on how you ship.</p>
<h3 id="do-we-need-the-review-tool-to-live-in-the-same-product-as-the-agent" class="anchor-heading group "><a href="#do-we-need-the-review-tool-to-live-in-the-same-product-as-the-agent" class="anchor-link" aria-label="Link to this section"><span class="anchor-icon" aria-hidden="true">#</span></a>Do we need the review tool to live in the same product as the agent?</h3>
<p>You can buy a standalone reviewer. Many teams do. The cost is context switching and a thinner view of how the code was produced. When review runs in the same system that wrote the change, it already knows the open files, the repo map, and the rules you maintain next to the code. Fixes can deep-link back into the editor or spawn an agent with the finding loaded. That loop is hard to fake with a bolt-on.</p>
<h2 id="how-to-run-ai-code-review-in-cursor" class="anchor-heading group "><a href="#how-to-run-ai-code-review-in-cursor" class="anchor-link" aria-label="Link to this section"><span class="anchor-icon" aria-hidden="true">#</span></a>How to run AI code review in Cursor</h2>
<p>Cursor&#x27;s path is local review in the editor, Bugbot on the pull request, then a fix loop that returns you to the same toolchain.</p>
<figure class="media-border-container overflow-hidden bg-theme-bg"><svg viewBox="0 0 800 280" role="img" aria-labelledby="ai-code-review-loop-alt" class="h-auto w-full" locally in the editor, then on the pull request, then back into a fix loop.</figcaption></figure>
<p><strong>Local.</strong> After agent work, run <a href="https://cursor.com/docs/agent/agent-review" rel="noopener noreferrer" target="_blank">Agent Review</a>. You can type <code>/agent-review</code> in the agent input, run it from the Source Control tab to compare local changes against your main branch, or turn on automatic reviews after every commit. Before you push, you can also run Bugbot or a Security Agent locally with the <code>/review-bugbot</code> and <code>/review-security</code> skills. This is where you clear obvious problems while the session still has context.</p>
<p><strong>On the PR.</strong> <a href="https://cursor.com/docs/bugbot" rel="noopener noreferrer" target="_blank">Bugbot</a> reviews pull requests on GitHub, GitLab, and Bitbucket. Encode team invariants in <code>.cursor/BUGBOT.md</code>, plus team rules and repo rules. Learned rules (<code>@cursor remember</code>) fold feedback into future runs. Watch resolution rate in Bugbot Automations before you widen comment categories.</p>
<p><strong>Fix loop.</strong> Findings show up on the PR with paths back into Cursor (Fix in Cursor and Fix in Web). Bugbot Autofix can spawn a Cloud Agent to propose repairs. For security, Cursor&#x27;s <a href="https://cursor.com/docs/security-agents" rel="noopener noreferrer" target="_blank">Security Agents</a> cover the two jobs: Security Reviewer checks PRs before merge, and Vulnerability Scanner scans the codebase at rest.</p>
<p><strong>Start.</strong> The docs cover setup end to end: connecting your repo, choosing which repos and people trigger reviews, effort level, and <code>.cursor/BUGBOT.md</code>. Follow along at <a href="https://cursor.com/docs/bugbot" rel="noopener noreferrer" target="_blank">cursor.com/docs/bugbot</a>.</p>
<h2 id="automate-the-routing-and-sign-off" class="anchor-heading group "><a href="#automate-the-routing-and-sign-off" class="anchor-link" aria-label="Link to this section"><span class="anchor-icon" aria-hidden="true">#</span></a>Automate the routing and sign-off</h2>
<p>Finding bugs is not the whole review job. Two Cursor automations handle the mechanical parts.</p>
<p><strong>Auto-approve low-risk changes.</strong> <a href="https://cursor.com/docs/approval-agents" rel="noopener noreferrer" target="_blank">Approval Agents</a> score each pull request by risk and approve the ones that clear the bar you set. A copy tweak or a config bump can merge without waiting on a human. Anything above your risk threshold is held. Bugbot and Security Agent findings feed that decision, so a risky change does not get waved through.</p>
<p><strong>Route to the right reviewers.</strong> When a PR needs a person, Approval Agents assign reviewers based on the part of the codebase it touches, using per-area routing policies you define. The change goes to the team that owns that code instead of a shared queue.</p>
<h2 id="keep-review-close-to-the-code" class="anchor-heading group "><a href="#keep-review-close-to-the-code" class="anchor-link" aria-label="Link to this section"><span class="anchor-icon" aria-hidden="true">#</span></a>Keep review close to the code</h2>
<p>AI code review is how teams keep a quality gate while agents increase the size and speed of change. The versions that work have repo context, a narrow comment policy, and a metric that tracks whether findings get fixed.</p>
<p>Review belongs close to where the code was produced, with the same rules and the same fix path. Turn <a href="https://cursor.com/docs/bugbot" rel="noopener noreferrer" target="_blank">Bugbot</a> on for a busy repo, watch resolution in <a href="https://cursor.com/automations/from-cursor/bugbot" rel="noopener noreferrer" target="_blank">Bugbot Automations</a> for a week, and only then decide which categories deserve more volume.</p></div><footer class="mt-v2"><p class="type-base"><span class="text-theme-text-sec">Filed under:<!-- --> </span><span class="text-theme-text capitalize">code review</span></p></footer></div></div></div></article><section class="mt-v3 border-theme-border-02 border-t pt-v2"><div class="grid-cursor"><div class="col-span-full xl:col-start-1 xl:col-end-7"><h2 class="type-base text-theme-text mb-v1 xl:sticky xl:top-[var(--site-sticky-top)] xl:mb-0">Related guides</h2></div><div class="col-span-full xl:col-start-7 xl:col-end-19"><div class="grid grid-cols-1 gap-g1"><article class="flex grow-1 flex-col"><a class="card card--text grow-1 flex h-full flex-col no-underline" href="/guides/model-routing"><p class="type-base text-theme-text text-pretty">Model routing: right model, right job, right price</p><p class="type-base text-theme-text-sec mt-v4/12 text-pretty">Model routing sends each request to the model that fits the job, so routine work stops billing at frontier prices. Review is most useful as part of the same system that produced the change.\"}]\n2b:[\"$\",\"$L54\",null,{\"as\":\"h2\",\"id\":\"what-changed-about-code-review\",\"children\":\"What changed about code review\"}]\n2c:[\"$\",\"p\",null,{\"children\":\"Coding agents did not invent long pull requests, but they made the old review math fail faster.\"}]\n2d:[\"$\",\"p\",null,{\"children\":[\"Developers working with coding agents are shipping bigger changes. \",[\"$\",\"a\",null,{\"href\":\"https://cursor.com/insights/developer-habits\",\"rel\":\"noopener noreferrer\",\"target\":\"_blank\",\"children\":\"Data from millions of Cursor sessions\"}],\" shows lines added per PR (p75) up about 2.5x year over year. Mega PRs of 1,000+ changed lines are a growing share of merges, with a clear jump in January 2026 as agents and models improved. Agent sessions got deeper too: mean tool calls per session rose about 30% in a recent two-month window. More of the AI-authored code survives. Accepted AI lines still present after 60 minutes rose from roughly 76% to 81% since the start of 2026. Agent-generated changes that reach commits without a separate manual diff-acceptance step grew more than 5x over that period.\"]}]\n2e:[\"$\",\"p\",null,{\"children\":\"Human review capacity did not scale with any of that. Classic peer-review guidance has long treated a few hundred lines of careful reading as the range where quality holds.\"}]\n2f:[\"$\",\"p\",null,{\"children\":\"AI code review is how you keep a quality gate when the volume of change outruns the number of senior engineers who can read every diff.\"}]\n30:[\"$\",\"p\",null,{\"children\":\"More of the code under review was written with AI assistance. Humans are good at catching \\\"this does not match how we build here.\\\" They are worse at staring down a large, plausible, mostly-correct agent patch for the one subtle break, which is where a reviewer with real repo context helps.
